The Phase 2 project involved retrofitting a Class 4 midsize, medium-duty electric shuttle by Phoenix Motorcars with AV technology provided by Perrone Robotics. The resulting vehicle would then have operated as a shared-ride, zero-emission, SAE Level 4 AV compliant with Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, Buy America, and ADA regulations. Despite the vehicle not reaching public operations, the project resulted in lessons learned and best practices that can be used by future project teams, for both Houston METRO and the Federal Transit Administration. In addition, Texas Southern University, a key academic partner, will conduct in-depth analyses of these lessons learned, supported by funding provided through the Houston-Galveston Area Council. Notably, when operating in automation mode, the Perrone Robotics’ TONY platform on the shuttle bus operated as intended without any issues or concerns. The vehicle successfully operated in autonomous mode, with passengers on board, during two demonstration visits and autonomously navigated within a METRO Bus Operating facility during the ribbon-cutting event in December 2023. 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Source: Houston METRO 3.2.3 Rivium District ParkShuttle The fleet of AVs operating at the Rivium business and residential district in the Netherlands, near Rotterdam, began passenger service on a dedicated transitway more than 20 years ago, operating in what was in essence an SAE Level 4 driverless operation during that time. The Rivium system operates without safety attendants and is representative of ATN technology provided on dedicated transitways. Of note for this early AV technology is the use of automobile and pedestrian traffic crossings that have “gate arms” (i.e., wishbone gates), control of which is integrated with the vehicle’s supervisory control system. The gate arms lower to prevent traffic and pedestrians from crossing the transitway when a fleet AV is approaching—a type of “transit priority” safety provision that has worked over the life of the system’s operations. Figure 12 shows this gate arm application in service for an at-grade roadway crossing. The gate arm controls conflicting automobile movements and various forms of micromobility movements by lowering wishbone gates when fleet AVs are passing. 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory
